finds.quote: The genuine/spurious partition of this corpus is an inference, not an attestation. Andronicus of Rhodes constituted it in the first century BCE — some 250 years after Aristotle — working, on the tradition's own account, from the cross-references the texts contain and from school documents. His catalogue is not extant. And his judgments have been overturned: he held *De interpretatione* spurious, and the field now receives it as genuine.

finds.note: Argues the received authenticity partition of the Aristotelian corpus is an inference by Andronicus built from the consistency at issue; partly received scholarship, but advanced against filtering by it.

finds.quote: I argue that it describes an operation, not an attitude; that the operation is an edition — the revamping and inhabiting of a received character; that the base of the edition is a circulating character whose named, quoted, surviving instance the corpus itself cites — the *Apology*'s Aristophanic Socrates, received ἐκ παίδων;
finds.window: Plato, Ep. II 314c; Apology, Clouds, Symposium, Parmenides
finds.note: Thesis that the Second Letter's 'Socrates become beautiful and new' describes an edition of a received (Aristophanic) character.

finds.quote: That the operation succeeded is a matter of record, and the record's first entry is Aristotle. The epilogue of the *Sophistical Refutations*, surveying what stood before its own inquiry, keeps the *Clouds*' pay-marker for exactly the class the base text fused with Socrates — τῶν περὶ τοὺς ἐριστικοὺς λόγους **μισθαρνούντων**, the paid teachers of eristic, dismissed with the shoemaker's analogy — and sets Socrates *apart* from them, named alone, keyed not to pay or teaching but to the confession of not knowing: Σωκράτης ἠρώτα ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι (183b7–8).
finds.note: Reception thesis: Aristotle and a Byzantine paraphrast inherit the repaired figure as settled.

finds.quote: The reception witness is dated by the canon itself: the thirteen *Epistles* stand as a body in the ninth tetralogy of the corpus's ancient arrangement (Diogenes Laertius 3.61), so the letter was read as Plato's by the early first century CE at the latest, and its description is evidence of how the operation looked from inside the tradition that transmitted it. "Earliest" is not claimed; *early enough to enter the canon* is.
finds.window: early first century CE at the latest
finds.note: Dating claim for the letter's reception as Plato's via the ninth tetralogy.

finds.quote: The only stone that names Aristotle names him as compiler. The only titles the catalogue carries that are attested outside the catalogue by a contemporary object are lists of victors. Andronicus made the corpus by making πίνακες; the Amphictyony honoured Aristotle for making one. Across the whole dossier, the act the record certifies for Aristotle from outside the corpus is the making of a registry.

finds.quote: So I shall argue: the two ghosts are one filing operation seen from its two sides. Each catalogue presupposes that its author could write in the other's mode and then ghosts the products, while the candidates for them stand extant under the other name, title for title. A tradition committed to two authors needs the ghosts, because without them the dramatic Aristotle and the analytical Plato would have to be found, and the only places they can be found are across the partition. A single corpus organized retroactively as two would leave exactly this residue.
finds.window: Diogenes Laertius III and V catalogues; Thrasyllus
finds.note: Thesis that Aristotle's lost dialogues and Plato's lost divisions are one filing operation; a single corpus organized retroactively as two would leave this residue.
